articles.title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow Big Bend border wall construction
articles.summary: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to clear the way for border wall construction to resume around Texas’s Big Bend region. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called a lower judge’s block on the construction “baseless” and said it disrupts the government’s ability to secure a quarter of the southern border. “Such judicial…
articles.body:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to clear the way for border wall construction to resume around Texas’s Big Bend region.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer called a lower judge’s block on the construction “baseless” and said it disrupts the government’s ability to secure a quarter of the southern border.

“Such judicial usurpation of Congress’s commands and the Secretary’s authority amply warrants a stay,” he wrote to the court.

Then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem waived environmental laws earlier this year to expedite the construction of barriers and roads across the Big Bend sector.

The administration has said it will not build a large border wall inside Big Bend National Park but is pursuing other construction activity there. It does still appear to be planning wall construction in other parts of the region, which sits along the bend of the Rio Grande.

The administration wants the Supreme Court to lift a ruling from U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone, who blocked the project earlier this month in response to a lawsuit filed by a preservation group, a recreation guide and the Center for Biological Diversity.

Cardone, an appointee of former President George W. Bush, found the construction is sizable enough where it requires clear congressional authorization.

The Trump administration points to a federal immigration law allowing border construction “to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry.” But the judge wrote that “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire U.S.-Mexico border.”

The administration has regularly turned to the Supreme Court for emergency relief after a judge has blocked an aspect of the president’s agenda, and the justices have sided with the president more often than not.

However, it hasn’t been a clean sweep. Earlier on Wednesday, the court refused to revive the administration’s restrictions for transgender inmates.

Sauer’s latest request asks the justices to also go a step further. In addition to granting emergency relief, which would technically be an interim decision, he wants them to completely overrule the judge’s decision, without waiting for the case to one day return to their normal docket.

“Those errors are so obvious that this Court can swiftly correct them on the merits without further briefing or oral argument,” Sauer wrote.

articles.title: US pulls personnel from Saudi Arabia as kingdom comes under Houthi fire
articles.summary: Trump weighs direct military strikes against the Houthis as deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia escalate and Riyadh urgently seeks U.S. interceptors.
articles.body: The Trump administration has ordered non-emergency U.S. government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as deadly Houthi attacks intensify across the kingdom, raising the stakes as President Donald Trump weighs direct military action against the Iran-backed group. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott confirmed Wednesday that the mandatory departure order applies only to Saudi Arabia, pushing back on reports that Washington was preparing a broader evacuation of diplomatic personnel across the Gulf. "The U.S. Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only," Pigott said. HOW SAUDI ARABIA'S DEFENSE VULNERABILITIES COULD BECOME TRUMP'S PROBLEM AMID HOUTHI ONSLAUGHT The order comes amid a surge in Houthi missile and drone attacks that has left civilians dead, disrupted air travel and sent Saudi Arabia scrambling for additional missile defenses. "Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," Pigott added. President Donald Trump is weighing whether to launch direct U.S. military strikes against the Houthis, whose expanding missile and drone campaign has increasingly threatened Saudi cities, airports and energy infrastructure. Houthi strikes and attempted strikes on Saudi Arabia more than doubled in a single week this month, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, with airports in Riyadh, Jizan, Najran, Dammam and Abha targeted since Oct. 5. The deadliest barrage struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing at least 13 people and wounding more than 300. SAUDI ARABIA ON EDGE: ICONIC KINGDOM CENTRE SENDS WORKERS HOME AMID HOUTHI ATTACKS The escalating attacks have prompted Saudi Arabia to seek additional military support from its allies. Britain announced Tuesday that it would deploy Typhoon fighter jets to help defend Saudi cities and critical infrastructure, while Egypt is assisting the kingdom and Israel has offered to help. Riyadh has also asked Washington for additional missile interceptors, though U.S. officials have warned that global demand is straining available supplies. "I also talked to Saudi Arabia today; they'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday. Rubio described the weapons as "probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field," acknowledging that the United States must balance requests from allies against its own military requirements. The growing threat has exposed the difficulty of defending Saudi Arabia's vast territory against relatively inexpensive missiles and drones, even with some of the world's most sophisticated air defenses. "Saudi Arabia is a huge geography to protect, and this speaks to a larger threat we're facing globally: a relatively small nonstate actor can pose a serious challenge to even a sophisticated and extremely expensive military," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House, told Fox News Digital in an interview published Wednesday. "The Houthis can impose enormous costs without having to spend very much themselves," he said. Trump has left open the possibility of direct military intervention against the Houthis, telling reporters earlier this month that the U.S. could join Saudi strikes against the group. "We may. We're gonna look at it," Trump said. "We'll make a decision. We move very quickly." articles.title: El-Sayed defends Slotkin over remarks targeted by right
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed (D) is standing by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) after the lawmaker sparked the GOP’s ire with a recent comment that she wants young professionals to rethink accepting a job with the Trump administration. In a Wednesday radio interview with “The Daily Blast with Greg Sargent,” El-Sayed accused Republicans of…
articles.body:
Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed (D) is standing by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) after the lawmaker sparked the GOP’s ire with a recent comment that she wants young professionals to rethink accepting a job with the Trump administration.

In a Wednesday radio interview with “ The Daily Blast with Greg Sargent ,” El-Sayed accused Republicans of attempting to “manufacture” a controversial moment over Slotkin’s remark.

“The way that Donald Trump has wound himself around the justice system is frankly unprecedented. It’s ugly and it’s antidemocratic,” the Democratic nominee said.

“And so I’ll take seriously what they’re up in arms about when they start taking themselves seriously around what Donald Trump is doing and every other congressional Republican just looks away,” El-Sayed continued, adding, “They’re not serious people.”

The Democratic candidate is running in a closely watched midterm race against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) for Michigan’s open Senate seat.

President Trump this week criticized Slotkin over the comment she made during an event at the University of Chicago over the weekend and accused her of having “weaponized government.”

“What they’re doing is really discouraging people from going into politics,” Trump said in comments to reporters outside the White House on Monday. “They weaponized the government, the Democrats — that’s what they’ve done.”

In her remarks at the Chicago event, the senator expressed her interest in investigating not only the president, but also the “people who enabled him” for alleged crimes.

“I want young people coming out of school to say, ‘Should I go work for the Trump administration? Like, that sounds fun. I might get an opportunity,’” she said. “I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want. And so, let me avoid participating in that.’”

“I want that deterrence message sent,” Slotkin added.

In a Monday post on the social platform X , the Democrat said her point was to warn young graduates that “there will be accountability for people who commit crimes on his [Trump’s] behalf.”

articles.title: Trump heads to South Carolina to boost Senator Darline Graham in race
articles.summary: The race between the sister of late Senator Lindsey Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews has tightened in deep-red state.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump is set to travel to South Carolina to boost the campaign of Darline Graham , the sister of his close ally, the late Senator Lindsey Graham.

The visit on Wednesday, which will include a rally alongside Graham, comes as the Senate race in deep-red South Carolina has grown uncomfortably close for Republicans.

Lindsey Graham, long one of the most hawkish members of the Senate who was an outspoken supporter of the US-Israel war on Iran, had been expected to sail to victory in the November 3 vote. But his unexpected death in July upended the race.

South Carolina’s governor tapped Darline Graham to finish her brother’s term. Trump then made the surprise move of endorsing Graham in a new Republican primary, helping her to claim the party’s nomination. The president said the endorsement was “in honour of her brother”.

In a video message last week, Trump again said Graham had his unconditional support.

“I’m asking everyone in South Carolina to get out and vote for a wonderful person, a great woman … a woman that Lindsey Graham said is the greatest person he’s ever met,” Trump said.

Democratic challenger Annie Andrews, a medical doctor and paediatrician, has seized on Graham’s inexperience and her unorthodox route to the Republican nomination.

Speaking to a local Fox News affiliate before Trump’s rally in Pendleton, South Carolina, Andrews pointed to Graham’s lacklustre debate performance, including one instance where she said she was “not that informed on national security”.

“My opponent needs the highest level of federal government politicians to speak for her. On the debate stage, it was really clear,” Andrews said.

Graham, meanwhile, has called Andrews “the most radical liberal that’s ever run for state office in South Carolina”.

Polls have shown Graham leading by about 2.7 percentage points, according to a Real Clear Politics average. Trump carried the state by 18 percentage points in 2024.

Trump’s visit comes after the president issued an executive order waiving most sanctions and tariffs on Russia, established by a law named after Lindsey Graham and passed with bipartisan support in 2026.

The move prompted a tempered rebuke from Darline Graham.

“Personally, I would choose to put the ⁠pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down,” she told The Associated Press news agency on Saturday.

“I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia,” she said.

The executive order on sanctions has been part of a wider Trump administration shift in its approach to ending the war with Ukraine, which began with Russia’s invasion in February 2024.

Trump and his allies have heaped pressure on Ukraine, framing its leader, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as the main impediment to peace. In turn, Washington has offered several concessions to Russia, including a deal to buy Russian diesel.

Lindsey Graham had been a staunch supporter of Ukraine. His death came shortly after he returned from his 10th visit to the country since the war began.

The tightening race in South Carolina underscores the harsh political reality for Republicans heading into the final stretch of the midterms.

Trump has sought to use his political clout to bring party loyalists out to vote, campaigning in strongholds across the country. But the president heads into the vote with the lowest approval ratings of his career, with voters expressing dismay about affordability and the knock-on effects of the US-Israel war with Iran.

Beyond South Carolina, other one-time Republican strongholds have shown signs of shifting towards Democrats.

That includes Kansas, where polls suggest Republican Ashley Hinson is effectively tied with Democrat Joshua Turek. The state, where farmers have been particularly hard hit by rising prices on fuel and equipment, has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1939.

Trump also broke from the Republican establishment to endorse Attorney General Ken Paxton over Senator John Cornyn in the Texas primary. Polling averages show Paxton, whose career has been marred by a procession of scandals, trailing behind Democratic challenger Talarico by 1.7 percentage points. The race is widely considered a toss-up.

A Republican has not won statewide office in Texas since 1994.

articles.title: DNC denies Bankhead’s claim she was offered job to drop out of Montana Senate race
articles.summary: Democrat Alani Bankhead said in a recent interview she was offered a Democratic National Committee (DNC) job to drop out of the Montana Senate race — an allegation the DNC denies. Bankhead is running against Independent Seth Bodnar and Republican Kurt Alme for the open Senate seat. She’s faced calls to exit the race to…
articles.body:
Democrat Alani Bankhead said in a recent interview she was offered a Democratic National Committee (DNC) job to drop out of the Montana Senate race — an allegation the DNC denies.

Bankhead is running against Independent Seth Bodnar and Republican Kurt Alme for the open Senate seat. She’s faced calls to exit the race to increase the chance of Alme losing the contest.

“They offered to be, and I’m probably going to butcher this, but the DNC’s head of female veteran candidates or something like that,” Bankhead said in an Oct. 15 interview with Montana PBS.

She stated her immediate response was, “Like, why would I go work for an organization that is actively working against me and stabbing me in the back? Like, no, I’m not going to do that.”

“And I can’t be bought anyway, but that was the only thing that was put on the table,” Bankhead concluded.

A DNC official told The Hill on Wednesday that Bankhead was never offered a job by the committee.

Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen (R) wrote on social media Wednesday that Bankhead’s allegation was “extremely concerning. If this is true, it appears to be a violation of Montana Code Annotated 13-35-221.”

Knudsen added that his office would be contacting Bankhead, Bodnar and the DNC to investigate.

Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) urged Knudsen to look into the situation in a social media post , writing: “Attorney General Knudsen is right to investigate this blatant attempt at bribery. The DNC is playing dirty in Montana.”

In a Washington Post op-ed published earlier this month, Bankhead wrote that 22 Democratic state legislators signed a letter asking for her to drop out, and she received a job offer from an unnamed U.S. senator, “presumably if I would leave the race.” She also claimed a Democratic governor contacted her to ask her to quit the race.

A spokesperson for Montana Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen (R) told Semafor in late July that even if Bankhead were to drop out, the secretary “took an oath to uphold the law, and Montana law plainly states that if a party’s candidate withdraws, that political party shall appoint a replacement.”

“That’s the law, not a suggestion. We’re not interested in political games,” the spokesperson continued.

The Montana Senate seat is one Democrats hoped to flip after Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) announced in March he would not be running for reelection. Early polling showed Bodnar could beat Alme in a one-on-one race; Bankhead has repeatedly said she would not drop out of the race to assist Bodnar’s chances.

Montana’s Democratic Party chair, Shannon O’Brien, resigned Oct. 12 and backed Bodnar’s bid for Senate, accusing Bankhead of not having the resources “or will” to win the Senate race.

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s election partner, found Alme has an 89 percent chance of winning the Senate race, with Bodnar holding an 11 percent chance as of Wednesday.

According to DDHQ’s aggregate polling, if the race had been held Wednesday, 41.9 percent of Montana voters said they would back Alme, followed by 29.4 percent who would vote for Bodnar and 17.1 percent who said they would support Bankhead.

articles.body:
Internet races to fend off newly discovered security flaws

The National Security Agency (NSA) warned organizations Wednesday to immediately patch a pair of security flaws or take their systems offline after artificial intelligence discovered vulnerabilities in a key programming language.

“Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities,” the NSA’s cyber division wrote in a post on the social platform X.

“These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database,” the agency continued. “If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommended that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.”

PHP is a programming language frequently used in web development and is often referred to as the “backbone of the web.” It powers 70 percent of all websites around the world.

Developers of the PHP language released fixes to the vulnerabilities Wednesday morning after government websites in Europe and elsewhere went dark, urging users to “update immediately.”

The bug identified by security researchers has been present in the code for 14 years, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said Wednesday.

A limited version of the bug was initially discovered in 2024 but wasn’t deemed significant, he noted. In August, security researchers working with an OpenAI initiative and using the company’s GPT-5.6 Sol model found a version of the vulnerability.

“Over the past two months, we have been leading a coalition to mitigate one of the most severe bugs in open source software found in recent memory,” Brockman wrote on X.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: Texas Senate race galloping toward a photo finish
articles.summary: Paxton's ratings are underwater by 17 points, while Democrat James Talarico holds a slim enthusiasm edge among likely voters
articles.body: Texas hasn’t gone blue in a statewide race in more than 30 years, but that streak could face a serious test this year. A new Fox News poll finds that while Texas likely voters favor Republicans retaining control of the U.S. Senate and give incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott an edge in his re-election bid, the Senate race remains deadlocked. The survey, released Wednesday, finds Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton tied at 49% each among Texas likely voters in the race to replace Sen. John Cornyn, who lost the GOP primary to President Trump-backed Paxton. Last month, Talarico was up by 2 points among likely voters (51%-49%). The shift to a tie reflects Paxton consolidating support among conservatives, rural voters, suburban women and voters who backed Cornyn in the primary. FOX NEWS POLL: TUREK, HINSON IN CLOSE IOWA SENATE RACE Although Paxton is falling short of Trump’s 2024 margins, he has strengthened his support a tad among both men (+1) and women (+1) since September, while Talarico slightly lost support (-1 and -2, respectively). Talarico leads by wide margins among Black voters (+65 points), urban voters (+29), those under age 30 (+28), and women with a college degree (+23). Paxton’s strongest groups include White evangelical Christians (+52), White men without a college degree (+32), rural voters (+21) and those age 65 and up (+18). The survey finds Hispanic voters swinging back toward the Democrats. After backing former President Joe Biden by 25 points in 2020, they favored Trump by 1 point in 2024, according to the Texas Fox News Voter Analysis. This key voting bloc now favors Talarico by 30 points (64%-34%) and prefers Democratic control of the U.S. Senate by 29 points. Overall, when it comes to Senate control, Texans choose Republicans by 4 points (51% to 47%), up from +1 point in September. Talarico’s stronger party loyalty is another reason the race is close: 98% of Democrats support him, compared with 90% of Republicans supporting Paxton. Nearly 3 in 10 non-MAGA Republicans cross party lines to back Talarico. FOX NEWS POLL: COST-OF-LIVING CONCERNS WEIGH ON GOP IN MIDTERMS Democrats also retain an enthusiasm edge: 69% are extremely interested in this year’s election, compared with 61% of Republicans. Extremely interested voters back Talarico by 7 points. "The race is going to come down to two basic questions," says Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who helps conduct the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "Do disaffected Republicans show up and, if so, do they grit their teeth and vote for a candidate who they have serious reservations about?" Views of Talarico are net positive, albeit by just 1 point (49% favorable, 48% unfavorable), while Paxton’s ratings are underwater by 17 (41% favorable, 58% unfavorable). Among "double haters," voters who view both candidates negatively, Paxton leads by 50 points. Voters express similar levels of concern about both candidates: 53% worry Talarico’s positions are too liberal, while 50% are concerned Paxton is too close to Trump. The intensity of these concerns is nearly identical, with 36% extremely concerned about Talarico and 37% about Paxton. In 2024, Trump won the Lone Star State by nearly 14 points, but his job rating is currently underwater by 9 points (45% approve, 54% disapprove). Still, Paxton draws support from 13% of voters who disapprove of Trump, while 6% of Trump approvers back Talarico. When it comes to their personal finances, more than twice as many voters say they are worse off (43%) than better off (20%) compared with two years ago; 36% say they are about the same. Voters who are worse off back Talarico by 45 points, while those who are better off (+49) or about the same (+26) favor Paxton. The governor’s race gives Republicans more breathing room: Abbott edges his Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa, by 5 points (52% to 47%), unchanged since September. Abbott has a positive job rating (50% approve, 48% disapprove), and nearly all who approve support him in the race, as do 9% of those who disapprove. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE Abbott also benefits from slightly stronger party loyalty and more ticket-splitting among Talarico supporters: 7% support Abbott, compared with 2% of Paxton supporters who back Hinojosa. Conducted October 15-19, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 2,011 Texas registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (205) and cellphones (1,303) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (503). Results based on the registered voter sample have a margin of sampling error of ±2 percentage points, and for the subsample of 1,398 likely voters it is ±2.5 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling errors, question wording and order can influence results. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population. Likely voters are based on a probabilistic statistical model that relies on past vote history, interest in the current election, intention to vote, age, education, race, ethnicity and marital status. Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: Gender gap and pocketbook pain shape Ohio Senate race
articles.summary: Sherrod Brown leads Jon Husted 52% to 47% in the Ohio U.S. Senate race, fueled by a major gender gap and Trump's sliding approval in the Buckeye State.
articles.body: Powered by a clear favorability advantage, a large gender gap and voter discontent with both household finances and President Donald Trump, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown has the edge over appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted in the Ohio Senate race. A Fox News survey of likely Ohio voters finds Brown leads Husted, 52% to 47%. Brown’s advantage is anchored by his stronger personal standing, with his favorability rating 2 points above water (50% favorable, 48% unfavorable), while Husted’s rating sits 13 points underwater (42% favorable, 55% unfavorable). FOX NEWS POLL: COST-OF-LIVING CONCERNS WEIGH ON GOP IN MIDTERMS More Brown supporters (88%) than Husted backers (83%) say they’re certain of their vote. FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON Economic unease creates another headwind for Husted because about 2½ times as many voters say their financial situation is worse than two years ago rather than better (46% vs. 19%). Those who say things are worse favor Brown by 49 points, while those who say their finances are better or the same favor Husted by 51 and 24 points, respectively. The president’s standing in Ohio adds to Husted’s difficulties. Trump won the Buckeye State with 55% of the vote in 2024, but just 43% now approve of his job performance. A 57% majority disapproves, with 46% saying they "strongly" disapprove. Meanwhile, 52% express concern that Husted is too close to Trump, including 38% who are extremely concerned. Brown faces similar concerns about being too liberal, as 50% are worried, though fewer, 30%, are extremely concerned. In the matchup, women favor Brown by 14 points, while men support Husted by 4, an 18-point gender gap. Brown also has advantages among voters under 35, voters with a college degree, union voters and those living in urban and suburban areas. Husted relies on rural communities, non-college White men and married voters and has a narrow edge among those ages 65 and up. Partisan crossovers further tilt the field toward the challenger. While Husted receives 90% of Republicans, 9% cross over to back Brown. Some 97% of Democrats support Brown, while just 2% choose Husted, and Brown carries independents by nearly two to one. Voters who view both Senate candidates unfavorably prefer Husted by nearly 20 points. Brown is up by 9 points among those who are extremely interested in the election and leads by 29 points among the 15% of Ohioans who say they have already voted. Legislative preference tilts toward the Democrats, with Ohioans dividing 50% for Democratic control of the U.S. Senate and 48% for Republican control. In the governor's contest, likely voters favor Democrat Amy Acton over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by 50% to 48%. Women favor Acton by 10 points, while men back Ramaswamy by 7, a nearly identical gender gap to the Senate race. The survey was completed before a negative television ad from Ramaswamy’s campaign featuring Acton’s estranged mother became public. articles.title: France in flames is preview of what 'DSA' Democrats want for US, senator warns
articles.summary: Sen. Eric Schmitt warns France riots preview what Democrats want for America while touting Boeing F-47 jobs and a St. Louis crime crackdown.
articles.body: The chaos engulfing France is a preview of what Democrats want for America, Sen. Eric Schmitt warned, contrasting the unrest with new manufacturing jobs and a federal crime crackdown in Missouri that he credits to cooperation with the Trump administration. "You see what’s happening in France. That’s exactly what they want here, the DSA Democrats," the Missouri Republican told Fox News Digital. His warning comes as riots, fires and looting have swept France after protests over rising living costs and strained public services turned violent, prompting curfews in parts of Paris and other cities. "I think the Democrat Party at this point is sort of post-American and anti-Western civilization," Schmitt said. VIOLENT FAR-LEFT RIOTS IN FRANCE ARE 'CHILLING WARNING' FOR AMERICANS AT HOME, MIKE JOHNSON SAYS With control of the House "up for grabs," Schmitt argued, Republicans need to make the stakes clear while showing voters what they have delivered. INSIDE THE HOUSE GOP'S 4-WEEK BATTLE PLAN TO SAVE ITS MAJORITY Asked what a Democratic House would mean for Trump’s agenda, Schmitt accused Democrats of obstructing Republican efforts on immigration, permitting reform and regulations. 'SQUAD' DEMOCRAT FORMALLY INTRODUCES BILL TO ABOLISH ICE, BORDER PATROL AND DISMANTLE DHS He warned that Democratic control could jeopardize funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and revive what he described as the political weaponization of government under former President Joe Biden. But Schmitt also argued Republicans need to give voters a reason to support them, pointing to jobs and public safety as areas where he says cooperation with the Trump administration is paying off. KEY AMERICAN INDUSTRY SEEING BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM AS TRUMP'S RE-SHORING POLICIES PAY OFF In Missouri, he highlighted Boeing’s selection to build the Air Force’s F-47 and the Navy’s next-generation F/A-XX fighter as a potentially transformative investment in American manufacturing. Boeing secured the Navy contract in September after winning the Air Force program last year. BERNIE SANDERS ADMITS DEMOCRATS FAILED WORKING-CLASS VOTERS ON ECONOMICS, DRIVING THEM TO DONALD TRUMP Schmitt, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said the programs would mean 7,000 direct jobs, with additional opportunities for suppliers and surrounding businesses. "It means that the goal we’ve been fighting for, which is that St. Louis is the defense tech capital of the United States of America, is coming true," he said. TRUMP SAYS POLLS 'DON'T ACCOUNT FOR ONE THING,' AS HE PLEDGES TO DEFEAT COMMUNISTS 'ONCE AND FOR ALL' Schmitt said he worked with Trump and administration officials to help land the programs, describing them as "generational opportunities" for Missouri workers. "You think of the good-paying jobs that’s going to mean for generations to come, it’s just a game changer," he said. He also tied the aircraft programs to the broader competition with China, saying the next generation of fighters would help meet military demands in the Pacific. On public safety, Schmitt pointed to Operation Show Me Justice, an ATF-led enforcement surge that resulted in 435 arrests and the seizure of 166 firearms in St. Louis, according to the Justice Department. Authorities also seized 81 kilograms of drugs and more than $1.25 million linked to suspected illegal gun and drug transactions during the operation, which officials announced had concluded Oct. 15. Schmitt said his conversations with administration officials have carried a straightforward request for his hometown. TRUMP’S LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS, GUNS IN BLUE CITY "St. Louis, we need your help," he said. The former Missouri attorney general described the toll of violence on families, including grandparents cleaning up broken glass and parents burying their children. "We don’t need to accept this," he said. "We just don’t need to accept the idea that violent crime needs to be in the headlines every single day." He pledged the effort would continue beyond the surge. "This isn’t a one-and-done deal. There are more resources coming," Schmitt said. OMAR'S NEW LEGISLATION TARGETING ICE SPARKS OUTRAGE WHEN THE INTERNET SEES WHAT'S IN IT: 'UN-AMERICAN' For families wanting to send children safely to school, visit a park or attend a Cardinals game downtown, he said the goal is a better quality of life. "I think the message is help is on the way, and there are real tangible results now, not just rhetoric, not just empty promises," Schmitt said. "We’re not letting up." Schmitt’s third major priority is modernizing St. Louis Lambert International Airport, an effort he linked to the region’s aerospace growth and aviation history. His Modern Skies Act would fund improvements to air traffic control technology, towers and airport terminals. He said midsize airports need help securing investments that larger hubs can more readily finance. "St. Louis is the gateway to the West," he said. "It deserves a world-class airport." The proposal remains a legislative push rather than a guaranteed funding award for Lambert. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said during an October visit that airport funding would be competitive. For Schmitt, those priorities form part of the argument Republicans need to make as voters weigh control of Congress. He cast the election as "common sense versus crazy," but cautioned that Republicans cannot assume their supporters will show up. "I think if we do that, we’re gonna hold on to the Senate, and the House is up for grabs."

I’m only doing it for him.” Yesterday in North Carolina, Trump vowed to instruct his Justice Department to settle claims by veterans regarding contaminated water at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune in North Carolina. “If we win the House and the Senate, I am directing the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible and get it off the books and get it finished,” Trump said. “If we don’t win, there’s no money. But in other cases, Trump wields executive authority to make good regardless of the outcomes. At nearly every one of his rallies, Trump touts his promise to send every American adult a $5,000 payment if Republicans hold the House and the Senate. But GOP leaders have made no such promise, and some key players on Capitol Hill doubt it would happen, saying they haven’t even seen a plan from Trump for where the funds would come from. A recent NBC News Decision Desk Poll found that just 14% of U.S. adults expect to receive such payments in that scenario, while 71% don’t expect it. Putin produced Hubbard at the perfect moment to build on his considerable advantage with President Donald Trump and generate favorable publicity. He could hardly have wished for anything better than to be described as a humanitarian by Witkoff, the top American negotiator.
